name: Tongues of the World: How Living Languages Spread
description: Where today's great languages came from and how they travelled: with scriptures, empires, printing presses and ships, and how small languages were written down or brought back.

checkpoints.name: Ancient roots
checkpoints.note: Sanskrit hymns are composed in India, and from its family will come Hindi and Bengali. Chinese characters appear on oracle bones, and Classical Chinese becomes the written standard of East Asia. Old Persian is carved at Behistun, Latin spreads with Roman power, and Tamil is written in southern India.

checkpoints.name: Scripture and empire
checkpoints.note: Arabic leaves its first inscriptions and then, carried by the Quran, spreads from Arabia across the Middle East and North Africa. Japanese gets its first long written work, in borrowed Chinese characters. Old English, German and French appear on parchment, the Cyrillic script is made for the Slavs, and Spanish shows up in monks' margin notes.

checkpoints.name: The vernaculars rise
checkpoints.note: Hindi and Bengali emerge as written languages, Russian is set down in Cyrillic, and Portuguese appears in documents. A Mandarin-type speech is written down in the Yuan era. In 1443 Korea gains its own alphabet, Hangul, and the printing press in Europe begins to fix national languages in print.

checkpoints.name: Across the oceans
checkpoints.note: The Spanish Empire carries Spanish to the Americas, and Portuguese goes to Brazil, Africa and Asia. Friars write Nahuatl and Quechua in Latin letters and print grammars of them. The British Empire begins to spread English, and on the East African coast Swahili poems are written in Arabic script.

checkpoints.name: Written and revived
checkpoints.note: Missionaries put the Maori language into writing, and a Cherokee silversmith creates a syllabary that his people learn within a few years. Hebrew is revived as an everyday spoken language, Esperanto is invented as a neutral tongue for all, and in China Classical Chinese gives way to writing in the modern spoken language.

checkpoints.name: One world of text
checkpoints.note: Mandarin Chinese has the most native speakers on Earth, while English, learned by vast numbers as a second language, is used by more people than any other. Swahili links much of East Africa, and Hindi is an official language of India. From 1991 Unicode lets computers handle all these scripts.
